cards.headline: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say

image.alt: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say

pages.text:
Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.” On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X. Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. Sunday’s strike on King Khalid International airport kills a Pakistani national. A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority. The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care. The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13. Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way. A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave. The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA. The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s. The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis. The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim. There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

Eight flights on the Dhaka-Riyadh route have been disrupted after King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia closed following attacks allegedly by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saturday, affecting 2,951 passengers, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (Caab). Of the affected flights, three were operated by Saudia Airlines, two each by Biman Bangladesh Airlines and Riyadh Air, and one by US-Bangla Airlines, according to the Flight Management System, civil aviation officials said today (11 October). At least 12 people, including two Bangladeshis and four Saudi nationals, were killed and over 300 were injured in the attacks allegedly carried out by the Houthis on the Saudi airport on Saturday afternoon. The airport authorities extended the suspension of operations until 9pm UTC today, equivalent to 3am Bangladesh time today. With no visible progress towards reopening the airport, Biman Bangladesh Airlines has suspended its scheduled flights BG339 and BG340 on the Dhaka-Riyadh and Riyadh-Dhaka routes for 11 and 12 October. The airline said it would inform passengers about the revised flight schedule at noon on Monday, Bangladesh time. Biman also apologised for the temporary inconvenience caused by the suspensions and sought passengers' cooperation. Zelenskyy says Ukrainian skies filled with Russian drones after truce claim, which Moscow has yet to confirm, as six killed in strikes. What we know on day 1,692 Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.” Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Russia’s military ⁠said it ⁠struck ⁠a logistics ​centre in southern Ukraine’s ⁠Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel ⁠in the ​Black ‌Sea. The logistics centre in the town ‌of Ternivka was used to ​store military and dual-use cargoes for the ⁠Ukrainian military, the ‌Russian defence ministry ‌claimed on Sunday.

cards.headline: Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine

image.alt: Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine

pages.text:
Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table."We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.Ties further deepenMilitary, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."Billion-dollar loan delayedIranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

Russian President Vladimir Putin declared his readiness to do everything in his power to help end the war in the Middle East. This commitment was made during a face-to-face meeting with his Iranian counterpart amidst stalled negotiations between Tehran and Washington, and increasingly close military and diplomatic ties between Russia and Iran. Russian President Vladimir Putin met with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan ahead of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit, which opened on October 9th at the Avaza resort on the Caspian Sea. "We are ready to do everything in our power to contribute to resolving this situation," Putin declared during the meeting. The Russian leader also acknowledged Iran's "genuine efforts" to end the war since the US and Israeli attacks began on February 28. Both leaders also highlighted "positive developments" in Russia-Iran relations. Since the conflict in Ukraine erupted in February 2022, the two countries, which face the most sanctions in the world, have steadily strengthened their diplomatic, economic, and military ties, becoming increasingly interdependent. These contacts took place against the backdrop of seemingly stalled negotiations between Iran and the US, with President Pezeshkian declaring talks with Washington "pointless" at this time, indicating that the gap between the two sides remains very large. Military relations are becoming increasingly close. The rapprochement between Moscow and Tehran is taking place in many areas, including military cooperation – a contentious issue. Ukraine and Western countries accuse Iran of supplying Shahed drones and short-range missiles to Russia for use in the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Russia is accused of providing data to Iran for use in attacks targeting US objectives in the Middle East. Putin and Pezeshkian also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan last month. Furthermore, according to the Iranian state news agency IRNA, in a phone call on October 7th, Putin told Pezeshkian that he was ready to support mediation in the Middle East conflict. The continued contact between the two leaders demonstrates an effort to strengthen bilateral relations at a time when diplomatic processes related to both the Middle East and Ukraine are facing obstacles. CIS and Russia's ambition to maintain influence. This CIS summit was attended by leaders from Russia, Iran (as special guests), Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Turkmenistan, and other Central Asian countries. Established in 1991 after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the CIS aimed to maintain relations and promote cooperation among the former Soviet republics. However, the organization has seen significant changes as some members have left or reduced their level of participation. Georgia withdrew from the CIS after the 2008 war with Russia; Ukraine ceased participation after Moscow annexed Crimea in 2014; and Moldova left the organization in 2023 as it strengthened its ties with the European Union. Against this backdrop, the conference in Turkmenistan was both an opportunity for Russia to strengthen relations with partners and to reflect the limitations in its ability to rally regional consensus. According to Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Center for Russia, Eurasia, and Europe in Berlin, the CIS helps Moscow demonstrate that Russia still maintains its own sphere of influence, strengthened through institutional mechanisms and regional relations. However, the conference also took place at a time when some CIS members were seeking to diversify their economic and diplomatic partnerships, particularly through strengthening ties with China and Western countries. cards.headline: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? | Explainer News

image.alt: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?

pages.text:
Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement. That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. The court was referring to Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law that prohibits any form of assembly or protest and had been enforced in key parts of Delhi ahead of the protest. Peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, especially outside areas where prohibitory orders under Section 163 were in force, the court said. The Supreme Court ordered that a notice board concerning the imposition of Section 163 in the area around its complex, should be taken down so there is "no apprehension regarding access to justice." It also ordered the restoration of Delhi metro and railway services, unless regulations were required to be imposed, keeping in mind disturbance to public order. The top court went on to add that lawyers and journalists should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties, after Saturday's police action saw several lawyers and journalists being detained along with the protesters. "It seems a competition in creating anarchy is emerging between Arvind Kejriwal and Rahul Gandhi. Whether it is the Aam Aadmi Party or the Congress, the country's revered voters have rejected both. Having failed to secure power through the people's mandate, they are now looking for excuses for their defeat," Swaraj told reporters. CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke railed against Modi in a post on X, shortly after the activist leader was released from detention on Sunday. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilization following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. pages.text:
The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. image.alt: Rooppur plant achieves first nuclear chain reaction in Unit 1 | The Business Standard

pages.text:
The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. Unit-1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant initiated its first nuclear fission reaction yesterday, marking a major milestone for Bangladesh’s first nuclear power project. The reaction, which begins a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, started at around 3:34pm after the plant received regulatory approval, Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, told The Daily Star. “For the first time, the commissioning team began the fission reaction at unit-1 today. We successfully started the process while every parameter performed according to design,” he said. The development marks the reactor’s first criticality -- the point at which it reaches a stable critical state at minimum thermal power and sustains a nuclear chain reaction for the first time. Project officials said engineers are closely monitoring reactor parameters, safety systems and control equipment throughout the process. The physical start-up phase, including first criticality, is expected to take about 30 to 40 days, after which power generation will be increased gradually based on test results. Dr Md Zahedul Hassan, managing director of Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd, explained that heat produced through nuclear fission would convert water into high-pressure steam, which would drive turbines connected to generators to produce electricity. Operators would continue monitoring the reaction to ensure compliance with all safety requirements and prescribed parameters, he added. If work proceeds according to the plan, the plant could begin supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis as early as next month, project officials said. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts (MW). Once both units are fully operational, they are expected to contribute a combined 2,400 MW to the national grid, diversify the country's energy mix and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Officials concerned with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) said the initiation of heat production through nuclear fission in the first unit had initially been planned for September. However, technical defects identified during safety valve testing delayed the next stage of work. Following two rounds of high-pressure testing, the results were submitted to the regulatory authority, which approved them last Thursday, the project officials said. The tests assessed whether the control valves were functioning according to prescribed standards. Fire safety and radiation protection arrangements were also examined as part of the process. The approval allows the project to proceed with further reactor commissioning activities. However, the officials said that achieving first criticality, gradually increasing reactor power, starting the turbine and supplying electricity to the national grid are separate stages, each requiring the completion of relevant technical and safety checks. The next major milestone is 'first criticality', when a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction is established inside the reactor. A series of tests and observations will follow - a process that could take around a month. Reactor power will then be increased gradually. Initially, the plant is expected to supply around 300 MW to the national grid on a trial basis. Further testing and technical assessments will be required before the facility reaches commercial operation. Built with technical assistance from Russia, Rooppur uses third-generation VVER-1200 reactor technology. Project estimates suggest that the plant could meet around 10 percent of Bangladesh's electricity demand when both units are operational at full capacity. Its actual contribution will depend on national demand, plant performance, maintenance schedules and grid conditions. Unlike coal-, oil- or gas-fired power plants, nuclear facilities generate heat through the fission of uranium atoms rather than by burning fossil fuels. The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electricity-generating system. Rooppur is designed for an operational life of 60 years, potentially extendable by another 20 to 30 years, subject to technical upgrades, safety assessments and regulatory approval. Routine maintenance and fuel replacement will remain essential, with refuelling potentially required approximately every 18 months. Sheikh Mohammad Touhidul Islam, joint secretary (Nuclear Power Wing) of the Ministry of Science and Technology, told BSS that Rooppur was not merely an electricity generation project but also a major opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's technological capabilities and develop skilled human resources. He said the first unit was in the final stages of preparation for generation, while uranium for the second unit had also arrived at the project site. He expressed hope that work could be completed ahead of schedule. Additional Secretary of the ministry Abul Khair Md Akkas Ali said the plant could reshape Bangladesh's electricity and economic landscape, supporting industrial production, attracting investment and creating employment opportunities. Science and Technology Secretary Md Anwar Hossain described Rooppur as a historic milestone for the country's energy security and economic progress, highlighting its potential to support reliable electricity supplies and peaceful applications of nuclear technology. cards.headline: Syria issues first letter of credit to Saudi Aramco in 14 years

image.alt: Syria issues first letter of credit to Saudi Aramco in 14 years | The Jerusalem Post

pages.text: The Central Bank of Syria announced on October 11, 2026, that it issued its first letter of credit in 14 years to facilitate a petroleum products supply deal between the Syrian Petroleum Company and Saudi Aramco. A letter of credit is a financial instrument used in international trade that guarantees a buyer's payment to a seller will be received on time and for the correct amount, serving as a mechanism to facilitate commerce between parties in different countries. This transaction was arranged in coordination with an unnamed major U.S. bank to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system. This move follows the United States' decision at the end of August to officially remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a designation Syria had held since 1979. The removal of this designation and related U.S. sanctions is viewed by Syrian officials as a step toward reconnecting the country to the global financial and economic system.

The central bank's announcement follows high-level discussions in New York on October 5, where Central Bank Governor Safwan Raslan met with officials from the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank to discuss account management and practical operations. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shibani stated that removing the state sponsor of terrorism designation was the last major obstacle to attracting foreign investment and rebuilding economic life in Syria. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the removal of the designation was taken in recognition of commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed Al-Sharaa to distance the country from international terrorism. President Al-Sharaa took power after rebels toppled former President Bashar Al-Assad in December 2024. Separately, the Saudi Arabian energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar, and Egypt on October 11, 2026, to strengthen energy cooperation.

cards.headline: Nepal flash flood washes away houses and bridges, with five people missing

image.alt: Nepal flash flood washes away houses and bridges, with five people missing

pages.text:
Some locals told The Kathmandu Post they had alerted one another to the flood nearly an hour before official notifications came in. Suna Gurung was awakened at 04:45 on Sunday by a call from someone in a riverside village upstream, saying a river had burst its banks and urging him to flee immediately. "Within ten minutes, the river swelled dramatically in the dark. We raised an alarm, woke everyone up, and fled into the forest," Gurung told The Kathmandu Post. "By the time I received the government SMS on my phone warning us to stay safe, we had already been sheltering in the forest for over an hour." Nepali authorities acknowledged the delay in alerting the public. Alerts were sent to residents in higher regions nearly two hours after the floods began, while messages to lower regions were dispatched nearly five hours later, they say. This, as with previous disasters, highlights the deficiencies Nepal's early-warning system faces, often forcing residents in rural communities to rely on informal networks and social media.

Nepal’s authorities ordered evacuations along the Budhi Gandaki River on Sunday, 11 October, after sudden flooding swept away homes and other buildings in the country’s mountainous north-central region. Villagers fled to higher ground as the swollen river surged through narrow valleys. Aerial footage released by the Nepal Army showed floodwaters racing between mountains and residents being evacuated to safety. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority warned communities to remain alert until late Sunday. No deaths were immediately reported, although several people were listed as missing. Preliminary accounts suggested the flooding was triggered when a landslide blocked the river near Chumchure, in Gorkha district, before the temporary barrier gave way. The latest emergency comes as Nepal struggles to recover from devastating floods along its border with China in August, which killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Nearly 33,000 people were affected, with around 7,500 homes damaged or destroyed. The government estimates reconstruction will cost $4.77 billion. Authorities are now focusing on restoring roads and bridges damaged in the earlier disaster, particularly in remote areas where disrupted transport links have made delivering aid difficult.

cards.headline: Ghana open for fresh evacuation of Ghanaians if South Africa situation worsens - Ablakwa

image.alt: Ghana open for fresh evacuation of Ghanaians if South Africa situation worsens - Ablakwa

pages.text: Ghana has not ruled out evacuating more citizens from South Africa if the situation in the country deteriorates, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has said. He said Ghana’s mission in Pretoria had submitted a report to the ministry describing the situation as “quite a dire situation”, amid continued anti-immigrant sentiment in the country. Speaking on TV3’s The KeyPoints programme on Saturday (October 10, 2026), Mr Ablakwa said the situation was partly linked to a recent decision by South Africa’s apex court on asylum seekers. He said the ministry’s Consular and Humanitarian Affairs Bureau was monitoring developments and assessing the welfare of Ghanaians who might require assistance. Mr Ablakwa said the government remained prepared to intervene if another wave of violence occurred and Ghanaians needed to be evacuated. “It does not mean that if we have another wave, a deterioration of the situation and there are Ghanaians who need assistance, it does not mean that the door is shut and that we will not move in. We will indeed,” he said. He said Ghana’s 72 diplomatic missions around the world were monitoring the welfare of Ghanaians in their respective jurisdictions. Mr Ablakwa said more than 6,300 Ghanaians had been evacuated from distress situations worldwide since last year, including from Libya, Myanmar and Cambodia. Of the total, 1,964 Ghanaians were brought home from South Africa during the most recent evacuation exercise. On Ghana’s petition to the African Union (AU) over the attacks, Mr Ablakwa said the continental body had responded and indicated that the matter would be placed on the agenda of its next summit in January 2027. He said he would not comment extensively on the latest attacks to avoid prejudicing the discussions at the summit. Mr Ablakwa, nonetheless, urged the South African authorities to take further steps to prevent the violence against foreign nationals from recurring.

cards.headline: Top NATO commander set to issue warning to Russia over any attack

image.alt: Top NATO commander set to issue warning to Russia over any attack

pages.text:
BRUSSELS, Belgium: NATO’s top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow. NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich — the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe — will elaborate his “theory of victory” over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw. The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s backers in the war against Russia. Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport. “The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance’s deterrence and defense plans,” Col. Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week. “But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” O’Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that. NATO — which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union — traditionally closely guards its defense plans to counter any attack by Russia. Grynkewich’s intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO’s strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance’s eastern flank. NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia. Western officials say that Moscow’s “hybrid attacks” have become more reckless as the Kremlin’s forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life. The alliance — whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion — has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict. NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep “calm, carry on and support Ukraine.” “We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger,” Rutte said last month. But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent. The results of the process are expected to be announced toward the end of the year. European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump. cards.headline: Planned pharmaceutical park in Ningo Prampram targets 30,000 jobs

image.alt: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest

pages.text: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations at the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a planned 2,000-acre facility in Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana. Developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority alongside the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), the project is expected to create an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority. Drugmakers have until October 12, 2026, to submit expressions of interest for the site. The initiative aims to address the fact that approximately 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is currently met through imports, which cost the country more than $300 million annually. The government has set a target to replace 50 per cent of these imports with locally produced medicines by 2030.

The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, intended to establish the country as a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and other regions. Under the development plan, a special purpose vehicle—a legal entity created to manage specific assets or projects—will provide shared infrastructure for tenants. This includes ready-built factory shells, cold-chain warehousing, an effluent treatment plant, and power, water, and steam that meet Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards. The facility will also feature a research centre focused on tropical diseases and quality control laboratories supervised by the University of Ghana. Tenants will pay fees or lease charges for these services, and anchor tenants may be offered equity in the special purpose vehicle, subject to final terms. Eligible applicants include companies producing vaccines, diagnostics, herbal medicines, generics, and active pharmaceutical ingredients, as well as joint ventures and consortia.

cards.headline: IMF warns of AI 'tsunami' hitting labor markets as World Bank council urges permanent employment support

image.alt: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’

pages.text: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that artificial intelligence is hitting the global labor market like a “slow-moving tsunami,” with young graduates identified as being first in line for disruption. Speaking at a panel during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva noted that the technology is already hollowing out demand for human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. The IMF estimates that approximately 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be augmented, downgraded, or eliminated by AI. Georgieva stated that while the technology can drive growth, it also risks straining government revenues by tilting economies toward capital and away from labor, which is a traditional primary source of tax income. She noted that exposure to AI is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, though she added that poorer nations are not necessarily better off, stating that the lower figure is “just because AI is further away.”

Addressing the impact on new workers, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to transform “crisis-era” support measures—such as those used during the Covid-19 pandemic or the global financial crisis—into permanent structural policies. Shanmugaratnam argued that these measures are necessary to help young people enter the workforce because the “first rung in employment” is seeing less demand. He noted that in the U.S., demand for graduates has decreased for the first time in a century, alongside a shrinking wage premium for college degrees. World Bank President Ajay Banga estimated that approximately 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years. Banga emphasized that because the private sector generates between 75% and 85% of jobs in any country, governments must focus on “de-risking” private capital—lowering the risks that deter investors from investing at scale—to ensure the private sector can absorb these new workers.

Despite the risks to employment, Georgieva noted that AI-related investments and trade have helped sustain global economic growth at around 3%. She estimated that AI adoption could add between 0.5 and 1 percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies, and between 0.2 and 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asian economies. Georgieva suggested these gains could “more than offset” the economic drag caused by aging populations in rich countries. Banga identified five areas with potential for job creation through AI and investment: infrastructure, smallholder agriculture, primary healthcare, tourism, and value-added manufacturing. He specifically pointed to Thailand’s tourism sector as an example of opportunity. While the first wave of AI spending has focused on infrastructure, Georgieva expects the next wave to be widespread adoption, which she said would allow more people to participate in the economic benefits.

cards.headline: A year after ceasefire deal, Gaza still waits for relief

image.alt: A year after ceasefire deal, Gaza still waits for relief

pages.text:
GAZA: One year after a US-brokered ceasefire was announced in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace. Israel keeps up its strikes and now controls about 70 percent of Gaza, while the reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” said Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City. “Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues, and we cannot even find a moment’s peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead.” On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing. Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the ceasefire. “We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats,” the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerricans of water back to his tent. Almost all of Gaza’s more than 2 million residents were displaced at least once during the war that broke out with the attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. With 82 percent of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, per the UN, many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where overcrowding and a lack of hygiene have led to outbreaks of disease. Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Yunis, said that he had yet to see the ceasefire take effect on the ground. “It has been a full year since the ceasefire was declared, yet it exists only on paper,” he said. Israel controls all entry points into the territory and continues to allow in only a limited amount of aid, which keeps the price of basic goods too high for ordinary Gazans like Ismail Hamouda. The 47-year-old father, displaced from Jabaliya in the north to Gaza City, ticked off what residents still lack: potable water, food, and financial assistance. “Here in the displacement camps, we thought that after a year of ceasefire, things would improve and get better,” he said. “Unfortunately, the situation is worsening gradually ... cards.headline: Wasauksing First Nation works to bring back wild rice — and youth are at the centre of efforts - MBC Radio

image.alt: Wasauksing First Nation works to bring back wild rice — and youth are at the centre of efforts - MBC Radio

pages.text: Photo: Group photo of Wasauksing Manoomin Youth and Survey Tour on Wasauksing August 2026 Wasauksing First Nation partnered with the Anishinabek/Ontario Fisheries Resource Centre (A/OFRC) this summer to assess the health and potential of manoomin (wild rice) habitats in the community. Close up shot of manoomin (wild rice). Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The aim of the project is to follow the community’s lead in restoring a food source that is central to Anishinaabe culture, food sovereignty and identity. In spring 2026, Wasauksing submitted a proposal to A/OFRC to support the revival of manoomin beds through scientific expertise and state-of-the-art tools while remaining grounded in the community’s own local knowledge. For Wasauksing’s Lands and Resources Office, success means more than ecological recovery — it also means “restoring personal and community well-being and self-determination; being able to manage and harvest traditional foods, strengthening our Nation’s food sovereignty.” The project aims to support the reclamation of cultural practices and traditional knowledge surrounding manoomin, while deepening community connection to land, water, and cultural identity. Through A/OFRC, Wasauksing has visited communities like Alderville to learn from Elders like Jeff Beaver, whose community has been running a wild rice reintroduction project since the 1990s. Gabrielle Perugini, A/OFRC’s lead fisheries biologist, said much of what they have learned as an organization and what makes these sort of restoration projects possible comes from knowledge keepers like Jeff Beaver from Alderville First Nation. Youth from the community spent a week alongside the A/OFRC team exploring local waters, learning the history of manoomin in their territory and getting hands-on experience with the monitoring and surveying of identified sites. “There were lots of smiles and laughing, lots of knowledge transfer and storytelling while we were out in the canoes checking in on the sites,” said Perugini. Monitoring turbidity and water quality at manoomin sites. Credit: Shania Tabobondung/Metroland The fieldwork encouraged the youth to be part of the restoration efforts by learning how to use equipment to measure water quality at potential manoomin sites. They measured and recorded pH, turbidity, sediment composition, and water levels. cards.headline: Ziope undertakes initiative to build a technologically inclined community, commissions self-help ICT lab

image.alt: Ziope

pages.text: The Chiefs and people of Ziope in the Agotime Ziope District of the Volta Region have undertaken an initiative aimed at building a technologically inclined community. The initiative saw the commissioning of a well-equipped self-help information and communication technology lab for the community basic school, aimed at providing all-round training for pupils. This would enable the pupils to study the practical aspects of ICT, unlike previously, when they only had the theory with illustrations on the boards. The Ziope Community, under the leadership of Dufia, Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV, instituted the Ngoryiza, 2024, to mobilise resources towards the development of the area. Noticing the significance of information and communication technology in today’s world, proceeds from the 2025 celebrations were directed at the construction of a lab. At the commissioning ceremony, Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV lauded the community’s enthusiasm towards initiatives aimed at enhancing the livelihoods of the residents. He identified their efforts towards the construction of a 4-unit nurses’ quarters to house staff posted to the community health centre, contributing to improved healthcare delivery in the area. He eulogised Rev Mensah Djokoto for providing forty desktop computers for the proposed ICT lab, which is furnished with an air conditioner, robotic logistics and an internet connection. “None of the public Junior High Schools in Ghana has this kind of logistics, as seen at the Ziope Basic School. I am happy we undertook this initiative to secure the future of our children and the Ziope community", he said. Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV urged them to continue to contribute towards such development initiatives, to drive development in the Ziope community. “In unity we will find strength and development. If you bring a cedi and I bring a cedi, doesn't it become 2 cedis? Will your Cedi alone be able to do it? So we must continue on this agenda and not be tired as we have identified another project for next year”, he said. Rev Mensah Djokoto explained that he was touched and took the decision with a friend to make such a significant contribution to the education of pupils in the community, in an attempt to give back to society. He said that a zeal to ensure the pupils have an all-round ICT education prompted him to add coding and robotics to the centre, hence involving the Ghana Code Club. The Founder and Director of Ghana Code Club, Ernestina Edem Appiah, said a practical curriculum beginning with digital literacy and computational thinking, artificial intelligence, coding, robotics and electronics will be deployed, targeting how to train the pupils in creating with technology. “The children will learn to build programs and animations using tools such as Scratch; they will explore critical computing with tools such as micro: bit. They will learn the foundations of robotics, and gradually be introduced to AI, including how AI works, how it can be used responsibly, and how they can use emerging texts to create solutions to problems within their own communities”, she said. “We strongly believe that coding begins in their minds. So even before a child becomes confident with her computer, we tell them how to think logically and identify patterns. Break problems into smaller parts, experiment, make mistakes, and try again. That is a kind of learning we want the centre to be present”, she added. The Member of Parliament for Agotime Ziope, Charles Agvbeve, lauded the initiative, underscoring the need for communities to champion self-help projects, helping the government to develop the country. He expressed optimism about performance in the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) would improve as the “Agotime Ziope District scored first in 2025”, urging pupils of the final year students of the Ziope Basic School to score 1 in ICT in the 2026 BECE. He advised that the ICT lab should be used as a learning centre for pupils from other schools in the enclave to enhance their training as well. The Volta Regional Chairman of the National Democratic Congress, Mawutor Agbavitor, was elated with the initiative, acknowledging their efforts to lead the way in developing their community. He was enthused with their choice of enhancing ICT training of the pupils, as ”ICT is no longer a luxury but rather a necessity. The jobs of tomorrow, the knowledge of today, and the competition our children will face, all require digital skills.” The community launched the 2027 edition of the Ngoryiza, hoping to raise funds to tackle other social needs of the community.

cards.headline: Four candidates, four visions: How Mississauga’s mayoral hopefuls would tackle affordability, housing, crime and transit | The Pointer

pages.text:
With the increased powers mayors across Ontario hold, the decision to elect a new one carries immense weight for each of Mississauga’s 800,000-plus residents. Mississauga’s next mayor will inherit a city at a crossroads, where the cost of living is climbing, housing remains out of reach for the vast majority and growing congestion is testing the limits of local infrastructure. Unique, complex dynamics have also forced crime to the top of the City Hall agenda. Four front-running candidates, each with varying amounts of political experience, believe they can take on the challenge of leading one of Canada’s largest, fastest-growing cities. Alvin Tedjo has served Ward 2 as a councillor during the council term now drawing to a close, and was joined by Dipika Damerla who has represented Ward 7. Both ran in the 2024 mayoral by-election against Carolyn Parrish, who was victorious and is now seeking re-election after serving as mayor for two years. The three current members of council are joined by Bonnie Crombie , who is running again after taking over the leadership of the Ontario Liberals following just over nine years as Mississauga’s mayor. Tedjo has almost four years of experience representing constituents as an elected official, all at the council level; Damerla has been on council for almost eight years and served as an MPP representing Mississauga for seven years prior to that. Both Parrish and Crombie were Mississauga MPs; they both served as the Ward 5 councillor and both have been mayor. All four of the front-running candidates (The Pointer is not featuring other mayoral candidates who are far behind in the race according to public polling) are prioritizing affordability, crime and transportation (moving residents across the city and the GTA). In addition, Damerla has also made accountability inside City Hall a main focus of her campaign. Their proposed solutions to the challenges Mississauga residents face offer voters contrasting visions, from how they would control crippling property taxes and create badly needed affordable housing in the booming city, to how certain types of crime plaguing communities should be confronted while not allowing police spending to break the backs of homeowners, and managing major transit and transportation projects to ease the city’s rapidly worsening congestion. While all four candidates recognize that affordability, housing, crime and transportation are critical issues—the priorities voters are focused on as they decide who will get their vote on October 26—the candidates are proposing different solutions to confront the most pressing problems. A Mainstreet Research poll, commissioned by Y Media, conducted at the end of September showed Bonnie Crombie was the top choice of voters for Mississauga mayor, but other candidates are only slightly behind her. (Mainstreet Research) A poll conducted by Liaison Strategies at around the same time also found Bonnie Crombie is leading Carolyn Parrish by a narrow margin with Alvin Tedjo not far behind. (Liaison Strategies) Property taxes emerged as one of the defining issues in recent debates over the past two weeks, with candidates pitching their promises to freeze taxes for differing periods, limit increases to the inflation rate, or find more creative ways to expand the budget at an affordable rate by finding significant savings through external financial oversight—Damerla has been pushing for this during the council term, but Parrish and Tedjo shot down her motion for an independent Mississauga auditor general role earlier in the year. Tedjo wants to freeze the City portion of property taxes (Mississauga’s amount gets blended with the Region of Peel property tax increase to establish the total amount) for two years. “I’m committed to freezing property taxes for every single family in this city for the next two years to make sure that people have the ability to live in their homes with dignity and not have to make the choice between groceries or taxes,” he said during the Food Banks debate. “This is the single biggest tool that the City of Mississauga has at its disposal. It’s the property tax rate.” His promised freeze typically ends up badly for taxpayers, who still see large increases from spending that is shifted to the Region, onto utility bills or, in some cases, to a range of user fees. Debt financing or clawing funds from reserve accounts meant for emergencies and critical needs are options to offset tax freezes, but also have dire consequences for taxpayers immediately after budget cuts are made to achieve a freeze. North of Mississauga, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown, when campaigning in 2018, championed freezing property taxes. The end result of years of successive tax freezes has seen some of the City’s most critical projects left behind , as projects like the Riverwalk flood mitigation plan, the downtown redevelopment project, a promised stadium Brown vowed to build, a tunnelled LRT into Brampton’s city centre, its first standalone university, a second hospital which requires a City Hall funding contribution, fire facility upgrades, transit infrastructure needs bottlenecking the system, have been shelved, delayed, or continuously underfunded. City Hall’s costs to homeowners, meanwhile, pushed a record amount of properties into tax arrears due to Brown’s failed fiscal planning . Freezing property taxes typically causes a “pay-for-it-later” crisis, when the price to catch up with delayed costs to run and maintain a city ends up being far greater in the immediate future. Tedjo is promising to allow eligible senior homeowners to defer property tax payments altogether until they sell their homes, when the amount owing would be recouped. He stumbled badly when peppered with questions and suggestions that his pitch is nothing more than an election stunt that would never get approved, and he could not explain how the deferral would work or how a range of practical problems with his idea would be addressed. The Bangladesh Bank released the figures on Sunday, showing that total external debt rose 3.65 per cent from $110.93 billion at the end of March. At the current exchange rate of Tk 123.20 per dollar, the outstanding debt is equivalent to about Tk 14.17 trillion. The decline in private-sector debt reflected reductions in short-term borrowing, buyers’ credit and trade loans. Seventeen years ago, a char emerged in Purba Naodoba union of Zajira upazila in Shariatpur. On it grew a village called Alam Kha Kandi, and in 2017, the No 122 Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School was built there on 33 decimals of land. Back then, the Padma river was nearly two kilometres away -- not visible from the school gate. That distance has been vanishing. Over the past two years, successive bouts of erosion have dragged the river steadily closer, and it now licks at the school's own grounds, just 50 metres from the building. Teachers, students and local residents fear what has already happened twice nearby -- in 2024 and 2025, two primary schools in neighbouring villages of the same union were lost to the river. Painpara Government Primary School in union was swallowed by the river in August 2024; exactly a year later, in August 2025, Rizia Amin Government Primary School, also in Painpara, met the same fate. On a recent visit, the national flag still stood tall outside the erosion-battered school on the Padma's bank. But the earthen edge of the school field was crumbling into the water, and several trees lay broken along the bank. Nearby, the collapsed roof of a building the river had already claimed leaned forlornly against the shore. Inside, the signs of panic were unmistakable. The tin fencing had been dismantled to allow for a quick relocation if needed. The partition between two classrooms had been removed, and the overhead fans taken down. In the open space that remained, two teachers taught two separate classes side by side, children seated on either side of the room. At that moment, young voices could be heard reciting after their teacher: "Our little river flows in bends and turns, in the month of Boishakh it has knee-deep water." The children studied with evident joy -- but the irony of the verse was not lost on the adults around them. Erosion anxiety follows the students constantly, teachers said, and with the school itself at risk, safety concerns run alongside the lessons. Staff must now watch the river even as they teach. "The river keeps eroding and has come right onto our school field," said Borna Akter, a fourth-grade student, speaking to The Daily Star. "Our school could break apart at any time. It feels very scary, wondering when our school will break down. If our school goes into the river, we won't be able to study here anymore. Where will we study then? We want arrangements made to protect our school." School teacher Naimur Rahman Khan said panic over the erosion alone had already driven at least 100 students away. "We also always have to remain anxious, because the school is at risk," he said. "Even after we go home at the end of the day, we have to phone local residents to check on the river situation because arrangements for relocating the school must be made before it is lost to the river. If the school could be protected now, even by dropping some sandbags, children could attend classes here without fear." Altaf Hossain Khan, the school's founder and chairman of the union parishad, said the area had been eroding for years. "The river has now come close to the school. We have repeatedly requested the Water Development Board, but they have taken no action," he told The Daily Star over the phone. "If nothing is done now, the school could break apart and go into the riverbed at any moment." Md Milton Hossain, executive engineer of the Shariatpur Water Development Board, said the erosion in Alam Kha Kandi had been reported to higher authorities, but that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures in char areas. He added that no No Objection Certificate had been sought from the BWDB before the school was built on the char, and that neither the district nor the upazila education departments had alerted his office that the school was at risk. "Even so, I will visit the area and take the necessary measures, subject to permission from higher authorities," he said. Zajira Upazila Primary Education Officer Bazlur Rahman confirmed the school was at risk. "We have made preparations to relocate the school before erosion occurs, and another site is being sought," he told The Daily Star. "I will also request the concerned department to attempt to protect the school from the erosion." When the school was established in 2017, the Padma River was about two kilometers away. Over the years, the river has gradually reduced that distance and now it is near the school grounds. The school building’s tin roof and fence have been left open due to the fear of erosion. Some furniture and essential goods have been removed. Student attendance at the school has also decreased by about 70 percent due to the fear of river erosion. According to school sources, Alam Khankandi village is located on the north bank of the Padma River. The river surrounds the village. The waterway is the main means of communication for the people there. As there was no school in the area, the government established the school there in 2017. Local UP Chairman Altaf Hossain Khan donated 33 percent of the land for the school. The school was named after him. When the school was established, the Padma River was about two kilometers away. In the last two years, river erosion in that area has intensified. This year alone, the river has moved about one kilometer north. Now, the river is close to the school grounds. The school is teaching in five rooms of a tin shed with a paved floor. The school authorities have opened the building’s tin and fence due to fears of river erosion. Some belongings have also been moved to a safe place. In the meantime, classes are being held in the open room. The school has 214 students enrolled in the current academic year. However, due to river erosion, an average of 50 to 60 students come to the school every day. Many local residents have moved to a safe distance as the houses around the school have been submerged in the river. At least 110 students have moved to different areas 8 to 10 kilometers away. Monica and Jonayed, fifth-grade students at the school, say they are afraid to come to school now. They fear that the school could disappear into the river at any time. They are also worried about where they will go to study if the school collapses. Shamim Khan, the acting headmaster of the school, said that this year has seen the most erosion. In the last two months, the river has come close to the school grounds. He said, “I worry every day. After school, I go home and wonder whether I will be able to see the school the next day. I have removed some belongings due to the fear of erosion. In this situation, the attendance of students has decreased a lot. At least 110 students have permanently moved to another area.” Local UP Chairman Altaf Hossain Khan said that after the erosion started around the school, he requested the local administration and the Water Development Board to take action several times. But no effective measures were taken to protect the area. This year, at least 350 families in Alam Khankandi area have been victims of river erosion. These families have lost their homes and cropland. Now the school is also facing erosion. When this correspondent visited Alam Khankandi village last Thursday, it was seen that the fence of the school building had been opened. Various items removed from the building had been kept in one place. Two teachers were teaching third and fourth grade students together in two rooms of the open room. A teacher was teaching a few children in another room next door. 65 students were seen attending the school from 11 am to 1 pm. Jajira Upazila Primary Education Officer Bazlur Rahman said the school in the village on the banks of the Padma River is at risk of erosion. They are monitoring the issue around the clock. Preparations have also been made to move the school to another location. However, alternative land has not been found yet. They are keeping an eye on the situation so that even if the school is a victim of river erosion, educational activities are not stopped.
