cards.headline: UK revokes refugee status of Syrian surgeon, raising deportation fears

image.alt: UK revokes refugee status of Syrian surgeon, raising deportation fears

pages.text: QAMISHLI, Syria (North Press) – A Syrian plastic surgeon living in London faces possible deportation after the UK Home Office revoked his refugee status, arguing that conditions in Syria have changed enough for him and his family to return, The Guardian reported on Sunday. The surgeon, who fled the former Syrian regime and arrived in the UK in 2016, lives with his wife and six children, three of whom attend university. He said that he feared returning because radical groups that had targeted him remained active in Syria. “I don’t believe Syria will be a safe place for me to return to,” he told The Guardian, adding that he doubted the current Syrian government could protect his family. The Home Office said in its letter that although Syria’s situation remained “complex,” changes in the country meant his fear of persecution and serious harm could no longer be considered well-founded. The decision is believed to be among the first cases in Europe since the fall of the Assad regime in which Syrian refugee protection has been revoked, potentially affecting other Syrians living in the UK. However, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) urged governments to refrain from ending Syrian refugees’ protection until significant improvements in overall stability are achieved. The UK Foreign Office continues to advise against all travel to Syria, warning that the security situation remains volatile, with unpredictable fighting, airstrikes and artillery attacks, alongside a humanitarian crisis and shortages of essential services. The surgeon’s solicitor, Manini Menon of Duncan Lewis, criticized the decision, saying conditions in Syria do not justify concluding that refugees can safely return. The Home Office said Britain would not return anyone to danger and that people would be expected to return when their home countries were safe. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. Those already homeless lived beside roads or in tin-sheet shelters on rented land, while others planned to cross the Padma by engine-run trawlers to rent land in Zajira or Munshiganj. Duluna Begum, 60, travelled from Digholi in Bikrampur, Munshiganj, after her daughter called her at night on her phone to tell her that her in-laws’ house was being devoured by the river. “I came here early in the morning with other people to help them dismantle the house before the river swallowed it whole,” she told The Daily Star. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” Maksuda Begum, 55, of Farazi Kandi in Zajira also came with helpers to dismantle her daughter’s in-laws’ house. For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. He once owned 25 bighas, where he grew ginger, garlic, and vegetables, and a trawler to carry the produce across the river. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. He is now building a shack on land lent to him by someone. “If the government gave a little space to live on khas (government) land, then I could somehow spend my life raising a house there,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. They are Ahammad Majhikandi, Mongol Majhikandi, Alim Uddin Beparikandi, and Majhikandi, leaving around 1,500 families homeless. pages.text: Heat and humidity have led to one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, with West Nile virus at a decade high Heat and humidity have led to one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, with West Nile virus at a decade high Los Angeles might be best known for blue skies, beaches and film premiers — but for the last several years it’s held another, unenviable distinction: the most mosquito-infested city in America . And this year has been especially nightmarish, thanks to a series of heatwaves and an extra-powerful El Niño . Locals have called it a summer of “ living hell ” as clouds of mosquitoes swarm backyards and leave diners at open air patios scratching their ankles. That double whammy of heat and humidity is making 2026 one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, causing a spike in cases of West Nile virus and raising fears that the nuisance bugs could spread other diseases including dengue , brought in by travelers. With moisture in this week’s forecast and overnight temperatures likely to stay above 50F (10C), there seems to be no end in sight for a problem that local authorities have struggled to contain for the last decade. “I’ve been here my whole life and the amount of mosquitoes I’ve seen this summer has been insane,” said one TikTok user in a video with more than 20,000 likes. “Everyone is talking about them … You can’t even go to your back yard. You can’t even sit in your car with the windows down. They’re infested everywhere.” Southern California residents have struggled all year to keep the winged bloodsuckers at bay. Some have resorted to sleeping in long sleeves after failing to kill off the mosquitoes that colonize their homes. Others have tried to seal off the cracks below their doors with towels . “It’s an absolute nightmare,” Truman Hedding, an El Segundo resident, told Fox 11 News earlier this year. “We invest a lot of money to live in a beautiful town like El Segundo. The last thing we want is to stay up all night fighting mosquitoes.” Los Angeles county has documented more than 180 cases of West Nile virus this year, according to the county public health department – the highest number in nearly a decade. And mosquito season is still far from over. “This year in particular for our area has been higher mosquito activity and higher disease activity,” said Anais Medina Diaz, communications director for the San Gabriel mosquito and vector control district. “We can attribute that to some connection to the environment and how warm it’s been this year – particularly because we had a very warm winter. Mosquito activity plummets when temperatures approach 50F overnight. But this winter was exceptionally mild, with heatwaves in February and March that allowed mosquitoes to stay active. The unusually moist and humid summer made it easier for them to reproduce. The region has sweltered under a record-breaking heatwave since early October, although forecasts show relief on the way. But the temperatures won’t drop low enough in most places to halt mosquito activity entirely, while coming rains will give them new places to breed. Southern California hasn’t always been such a mosquito hotspot. The region’s most common endemic mosquito, the Culex quinquefasciatus – often referred to by the more easily pronounceable name “quinx” – prefers to target birds over humans. That preference exposes quinx to West Nile virus after biting birds, such as crows, known to host the disease. Infected quinx can then spread the disease to humans when they do bite them. The Orange county mosquito and vector control district monitors disease threats with a massive array of traps scattered throughout the area. So far, some 850 of them have tested positive for West Nile virus, according to the control district’s public information officer, Brian Brannon. “That doesn’t mean 850 mosquitoes – that means 850 traps full of mosquitoes with West Nile virus,” Brannon said. “We’ve had a pretty busy season.” The mosquito that southern Californians are most likely to notice, however, are those from the Aedes genus , which first showed up in the region back in 2014 and have proliferated ever since. Known locally as “ankle biters”, Aedes mosquitoes target humans. Because the mosquito is new to the area and people have had less exposure, Aedes bites can leave larger welts, according to Medina Diaz. “They like human blood,” she said. “They will bite you multiple times to get a full blood meal.” Aedes are not associated with West Nile virus, but they are known spreaders of diseases including dengue, chikungunya , Zika and yellow fever . One of the most effective ways to combat mosquitoes, and by far the cheapest, is to eliminate those stagnant puddles of water. A prized second-century artwork from the famed Fayoum portraits, known as the "Tondo of the Two Brothers", was unveiled following restoration in Egypt on Sunday. Specialists from Rome worked alongside conservators at the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir — where the collection is typically housed — for three weeks to restore the piece, officials announced at a press conference. Fayoum mummy portraits were created primarily on thin wooden panels and placed over the faces of the dead inside mummy wrappings, merging Egyptian funerary traditions with wider Greco-Roman artistic influences. Egypt is set to lend a significant portion of the collection to a temporary exhibition in Rome, marking the first time it will travel abroad. “The restoration of the Tondo of the Two Brothers is an important example of what can be achieved through international cooperation in the preservation and study of cultural heritage,” said Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s minister of tourism and antiquities. “Egypt and Italy share deep historical and cultural ties, and this project brings together Egyptian and Italian expertise to preserve an exceptional work of art for future generations.” Experts describe the painting as unusual because of its circular shape and its depiction of two people instead of one, and rank it among the most vivid surviving portraits from Roman-era Egypt. It was painted using a technique in which pigments are mixed with molten wax, and restorers were able to recover the features of the brother on the right. Aly Abdel Halim, director general of the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, said the conservation required careful intervention because both the wooden support, damaged by termites, and the painted surface were fragile. The portraits will be featured in an exhibition in Rome from November to May 2027. Tomaso Radaelli, chairman of MondoMostre, the exhibition’s organizer, said it will bring together more than 110 objects, including painted panels, funerary shrouds, masks, marble portraits, plaster casts and ancient jewelry.

cards.headline: As rising waters flood homes and temples, villagers protest India’s US$87 billion river-linking project | The Straits Times

pages.text:
Submerged trees in the catchment area of the Ken River near the Majhgawan Dam in Ajaygarh, Madhya Pradesh state, on Sept 20. AJAYGARH, India – Standing knee-deep in the Ken River, with mud smeared on her face to symbolise a connection to land her family has farmed for more than a century, Bitti Bai Kondar is among hundreds of tribal residents voicing anger over an US$87 billion (S$111 billion) government project to link India’s rivers. The mother of four adult sons, who are all protesting with her, has watched as rising water from work on the project has flooded her village. But the protesters say they would rather die than leave their ancestral home without better compensation. “The government is taking our land and water without giving us another place to live,” said Kondar, who is among scores of women who have shown their defiance by lying on mock funeral pyres. “They’re digging up our soil to build their dam, but they’re not giving us enough compensation to rebuild our lives.” The dispute is an early test for India’s ambitious plan to link some 30 rivers nationwide, which has been decades in the making but gathered momentum only in recent years, championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The aim is to redistribute water to drought-prone regions, boosting food security by aiding tens of millions of farmers in a country where agriculture remains a major employer. Critics say the programme risks uprooting communities and damaging fragile ecosystems. Connecting Madhya Pradesh state’s Ken River to Uttar Pradesh state’s Betwa River is phase one, with a cost of about US$4.6 billion. The government has offered residents along the Ken River in Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, at least 1.25 million Indian rupees (S$16,500) a hectare, more than double the initial offer of 500,000 rupees. Usha Parmar, the district administrator, said compensation to over 90% of people had already been paid. However, some residents argue that the payments do not cover all their losses. Dhaniram Bhatnagar, a local priest, said the temple where he worked had been completely submerged. “The temple was my only source of income and now it is gone,” he said. “The compensation offered by the government is only for my home, and that is not enough.” Environmentalists have long opposed the project, saying the proposed 2km-long Daudhan Dam on the Ken River will inundate some 9,000ha of land, including a significant portion of the Panna Tiger Reserve, one of India’s most successful tiger conservation programmes. The government has said the environmental impact is “unavoidable”, but can be mitigated through tree planting, wildlife conservation and other measures. Some critics even question the scientific basis for the multibillion-dollar plan. “There is a big question mark over this project’s feasibility because it rests on a hydrological presumption: a surplus in the Ken basin and a deficit in the Betwa basin,” said Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People. “That presumption has never been conclusively established.” A government spokeswoman said she could not immediately comment on the scientific assumptions underpinning the project and referred Reuters to an Aug 21 statement that said the project would help address chronic water scarcity in the Bundelkhand region, providing irrigation, drinking water and hydropower. In Mozambique , freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014 , a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique . However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience. In music, for example, this contradiction is clear. Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo . More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s , but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party. Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces. Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?” This is not just a provocative artistic comment. It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences. Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically. While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum , digital platforms for monitoring local governance , cultural associations, and artistic initiatives. This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces. However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order. One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools . The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered. By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity. During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest. In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions. However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent. In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity. When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk. This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.” Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost. Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival. In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value. It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity. The Mozambican Constitution affirms the right of all citizens to freedom of expression and opinion. But a democracy is not measured only by rights on paper, but also by the real conditions in which they can be exercised. The anthology brings together the works of several historical saints, scholars, unlettered poets, and voices of Kashmir, ranging from the fourteenth century to the contemporary era. In a conversation with Scroll, Drabu spoke about the making of The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature , the inspiration for the project, the process of collecting literary works from earlier centuries and selecting texts for an anthology of this scale. How did you get the idea to compile The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature ? I started my journey into exploring Kashmiri language and literature way back in 2013. That is when I started drawing the earliest illustrations of proverbs for something called Lipton Chai Blog . In fact, Scroll was the first platform to feature some of these. Those were the early days of memes and they got very popular. It was then that I started reading Kashmiri literature in translation and a few years later, started working on my first book on Kashmiri folklore. Starting then, I began reading a lot more. I could not read and write in Kashmiri, as during my time in school there was no Kashmiri in the curriculum, so it took me a bit of effort to learn the script and get quick at reading. When the publisher came with a suggestion to compile The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, I was already thinking about Kashmiri-to-English translation. I had worked on an essay for a book titled Violent Phenomenon , which collected essays around the topic of decolonising translation. I wrote about translation and the powers that determine what is translated, how it is translated and who gets published in the first place. It was a piece on the literary translation landscape in Kashmir, considering the various dynamics the language operates under – especially keeping the orality inherent in the language at its centre. I thought it was a serendipitous moment to actually define what a compilation, an ideal compilation, of Kashmiri literature could be. That is how I first drew up the table of contents of what would be the book. I had a few aims with this: I wanted to keep poetry and rhyme inherent in the language at the centre of it. I wanted all genres represented. I wanted a range of writers – those who publish within the traditional publishing ecosystem and outside of it. I also wanted a range of translators and translation styles – many of them for whom translation is beyond the remit of their daily work and profession. So it is an assemblage of translators, genres, types of writers, and styles of translation across a period of time. How did you collect these poems and literary works from the old centuries, and what difficulties did you face during the process? Were there particular sources or works that were especially difficult to trace or access? I think collecting the works was the easier part, but the labour involved in anthologising over these last few years was wider, especially with the range of writers and translators involved in the book – across geographies, time zones, and time periods. I started with reading literary histories, in Kashmiri, English, and Urdu. And then reading and mapping a whole range of literature in translation. From amongst what existed, I wrote to translators whose work spoke to me and then together we put together what they would like to translate or were working on already and how to bring it together. I write about the privilege of time and of resources I had at hand to put something like this together, but most importantly, the privilege of having guides along the way who I could turn to. Among the senior translators, I often asked translator Neerja Mattoo for her opinion, bounced ideas off her to sense-check them, and really, every single translator in their own way was a guide. Drawing on her edited volume, The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature , she speaks about language loss, the stigma around speaking Kashmiri, and the renewed interest among younger Kashmiris in reclaiming the language. Drabu discusses how oral traditions, folklore, Sufi poetry and songs preserve Kashmiri history and identity. She explains why The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature brings together writing from the 14th century to the present through themes rather than chronology, and why translators are central to the book. The conversation also looks at the lack of patronage for Kashmiri writers, the growth of Kashmiri content on digital platforms, and the role of language in preserving memory, belonging and home. Home - Breaking News - When There Is No Water: How Cross River Health Facilities Struggle To Save Lives But inside some healthcare facilities, the absence of a reliable water supply is creating another layer of difficulty for both patients and the health workers treating them. Bassey Ikor works at Atan Onoyom Primary Healthcare Centre (PHC) in Odukpani Local Government Area (LGA) of Cross River State; her biggest challenge is water, among others such as poor infrastructure, shortage of supplies, electricity, and manpower. Her plight is shared by many PHCs in the state, especially those in rural areas; water is not taken for granted. It is something health workers have to look for, at all costs. Before a nurse can attend to a patient, before a cleaner can wash a contaminated surface, before a mother can be assisted during childbirth or a wound can be properly dressed, there is a basic question that must sometimes be answered first: Where will the water come from? For patients who arrive at public health facilities seeking treatment, water may seem like the least of their concerns. They come with fever, wounds, pregnancy complications, sick children or other conditions requiring immediate attention. But inside some healthcare facilities, the absence of a reliable water supply is creating another layer of difficulty for both patients and the health workers treating them. This investigation examines how unreliable access to water is affecting the day-to-day operation of selected public health facilities in Cross River State, and what the shortage means for hygiene, infection prevention, maternal and child healthcare and the safety of patients and healthcare workers. At the centre of the investigation is a simple question: How can a health facility safely provide healthcare when it cannot reliably provide one of the most basic requirements for healthcare, water? Healthcare workers depend on water for almost everything that happens inside a functioning health facility. “They need it to wash their hands before and after attending to patients, clean labour room, wards, wash medical equipment, clean wounds, maintain toilets and dispose of waste safely. But when there is no water, many things can go wrong.” Jacob Onoyom, a retired school teacher, told TheInvestigator . For a woman giving birth, water is part of what she needs, especially after delivery. For a child being treated for illness, it is part of the basic hygiene that should surround that treatment. Joy Inyang recounts her experience. “I remember delivering at that health centre two years ago; if not for the rain, I wondered what we would have done because the facility had very little water. During labour, some women bleed a lot; some pass faeces, sweat and many other things will make you need water. We are close to the river here in Atan Onoyom, but we lack water, not to talk of clean water.” Like Atan Onoyom, in Aningeje in Akamkpa LGA, the story is the same: decayed infrastructure, no fence, lack of medications, few hands, and no electricity. Asuquo Inyang, a resident in Aningeje, described it as “poor working conditions”, saying: “When there is no water, it becomes critical for health workers to provide services because they need to wash hands before and after every patient they attend.” Idara Umoh, a mother of four who trades in vegetables by the market before the facility, said the situation of the PHC is worrisome because “It doesn’t look good at all and as you can see, the roof is leaking, and beds, no light and worst of all, water is a problem.” When the supply fails, however, healthcare workers have to improvise. In some facilities, this may mean relying on stored water, purchasing water with scarce facility resources or asking patients and their relatives to help provide it, like the case of the PHC in Odukpani Central, where they buy from a commercial vendor for 300 naira per 20 litres. The PHC in Odukpani Central draws water from a contaminated well beside their facility, which is only available during raining session. While in Atan Onoyom, it is the contaminated river they rely on. The PHC in Odukpani sits beside a new water project by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, Senator representing Cross River South in the red chambers, but yet to be commissioned. The consequences can go beyond inconvenience. A health worker who has to ration water cannot operate in the same conditions as a facility with a dependable source. A patient who comes to a healthcare facility should not have to worry about whether there is enough water for basic sanitation. Yet for over 27 PHCs in Central and Southern Senatorial Districts of Cross River visited by TheInvestigator, that question remains part of the daily reality. The findings by this reporter contradict recent claims by the state government that over 100 PHCs were beefed up across the state. The State Commissioner for Health, Dr Henry Egbe Ayuk, while briefing journalists in his office in Calabar in June 2026, made the disclosure. For Mwalimu Idowu, CEO of KaaAfrika Smart Tech Ltd, a company working in health, real estate and technology, the problem goes beyond the absence of functioning water facilities. He sees it as a failure of basic public service delivery. “As a concerned citizen, I would tell you that it is a combination of many things that have gone wrong,” Idowu said. cards.headline: This Carleton University exhibition envisions a Cree 'utopia'

image.alt: This Carleton University exhibition envisions a Cree 'utopia'

pages.text: What if the syllabics of the Cree language dominated everyday communication? This is the question asked by Joi T. Arcand’s new exhibition at the Carleton University Art Gallery. A key feature of the exhibition, which will run until Dec. 13, is a mural portraying a convenience store with signs rendered in Cree syllabics. Arcand says she was inspired by the Cree language's lack of visibility in Canadian society. "English or French is expected of us. We should have the same kind of access and representation of our own languages," she told CBC. "I got the idea to create this sort of utopic future, or alternate present, where our languages are in a healthy state." Arcand is an internationally renowned artist from Muskeg Lake First Nation in Saskatchewan. Her work has been exhibited across Canada and in Australia, South Korea and the United States. She's the former director of SAW Gallery’s Nordic Lab in Ottawa and has also worked on curatorial projects in Sweden. Arcand has been working on the current exhibition for four years alongside the Carleton art gallery’s acting director, Heather Anderson. The gallery is nearing its 35th anniversary and holds more than 30, 000 pieces of art in its collection. Anderson told CBC that Arcand’s work with Cree syllabics emerged from a 2009 photography called Here on Future Earth, where Arcand used photo-editing software to project signs with the language of Plains Cree onto buildings in Saskatchewan. Increasing visibility of Indigenous language is evident elsewhere on Carleton’s campus, including the renaming of the University Centre to Nideyinàn and Robertson Hall to Pigiarvik (ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᒃ). A billboard erected at the corner of Somerset and Preston features features the word 'aki' which means 'territory" in Algonquin. (Gregory Conway/CBC) Billboards featuring Arcand’s work will be erected elsewhere in Ottawa. One is inspired by the iconic Civic Pharmacy sign on Carling Avenue. Arcand collaborated with Anishinàbe artist Dani Printup on the billboard at the corner of Somerset and Preston streets. The billboard reads "aki," which is the Algonquin word for territory. Arcand told CBC that she wanted to use that language on the billboards to acknowledge the local Algonquins, saying their language and culture suffers from a lack of representation in the capital. Magnets featuring Cree syllabics add an interactive element to the exhibit. (Gregory Conway/CBC) The gallery exhibition also features interactive pieces including magnetic Cree syllabics placed beside Cree dictionaries and other information, allowing visitors to discover the language in a hands-on way. It also includes a payphone that Arcand collaborated on with Artengine, an artist-run centre in Ottawa that provided technological support. The phone rings when visitors trigger a motion sensor, and when they pick up the receiver they can hear Cree spoken by a number of people who are themselves learning the language. While Arcand has been working with the aesthetics and visual imagery of Cree syllabics, she says this was a new opportunity to venture into the world of sound. "I wanted people to not only see how beautiful the language is. I wanted them to hear it as well," she told CBC. Gregory Conway is a reporter from Curve Lake First Nation. cards.headline: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews

image.alt: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews

pages.text: Dawn comes early in Phuoc Hai, in Ho Chi Minh City’s Vung Tau area. At around 6 am, small round basket boats return to shore after a night at sea, carrying catches of fish, squid, shrimp and crabs. The sight of the little circular boats against the blue water has become a defining feature of the fishing village beneath Minh Dam Mountain. As the boats reach shore, fishermen hurry to untangle their nets and sort their seafood to keep it fresh before taking it to market. Nguyen Ngoc Chau, 55, was visibly disappointed after returning from a night at sea with only a few crabs. “Seafood catches have fallen significantly in recent years,” he said. “We used to earn an average of VND 500,000 (about USD 19) a night. Now we make only around VND 200,000 (about USD 7.70).” Nguyen, 46, who has been part of the village since childhood, said about 80 per cent of residents depended on fishing for their livelihoods. “Things are different now. There are fewer fish. Those who can afford it have replaced their basket boats with larger vessels equipped with GPS, fish-finding equipment and radios so they can fish farther offshore. Those of us who fish close to shore earn very little,” he said. More than a century after its establishment, Phuoc Hai continues to follow the rhythms of life at sea. After selling their catch, fishermen return home to mend nets and rest before preparing their gear for the next trip in the late afternoon or evening. Le Huu Duc, 58, said basket boats used relatively little fuel but yielded smaller catches. On calm days, he might bring home several dozen kilos of fish; in rough seas, the catch could fall to just 5-7kg. He said he had to make two trips a day to earn enough to support his three-member household. cards.headline: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk

image.alt: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk

pages.text: edited by Sadie Harley , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. The research was led by scientists from the University of Chicago, Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Bonn and Ohio University. Using high-resolution microCT imaging, the team reconstructed the skull and skeletal anatomy of the fossil. They discovered an unexpected combination of traits. Megacauda had specialized blade-like cheek teeth resembling those of modern seals, a platypus-like pelvis and an otter-like tail, indicating it was likely a semiaquatic predator that hunted small vertebrates and invertebrates in freshwater environments. More significantly, the researchers identified a pair of small bony projections on the roof of the mouth that closely resemble features found in living therian mammals, a group that includes marsupials (such as kangaroos and opossums) and placental mammals (such as elephants and humans). In modern mammals, these structures help support the soft palate and muscles involved in suckling, swallowing and protecting the airway. Because soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, scientists have long struggled to determine when these important feeding structures first evolved. "The anatomy of Megacauda suggests that structures involved in coordinating swallowing and sucking had already begun to evolve by the Middle Jurassic. This discovery helps us better understand the biological foundations of one of the defining characteristics of mammals: feeding young with milk," said Zhe-Xi Luo, Ph.D., professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study. The researchers also found highly specialized hyoid bones in the throat region. In living mammals, these bones help anchor muscles for swallowing. Together, the evidence suggests that Megacauda likely possessed an early version of the coordinated muscular system used by modern mammals to move milk and food safely from the mouth to the esophagus. The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about how these structures evolved. Researchers found that the newly identified therian-like bony hooks existed alongside more primitive bony ridges known from earlier mammaliaforms and mammalian ancestors. Their coexistence in the same animal suggests the modern structures did not evolve directly from the primitive ridges as previously believed. "This fossil captures an important stage in mammalian evolution," said Luo. "For decades, scientists have wanted to know when the soft-tissue structures necessary for suckling and complex swallowing first appeared. Megacauda provides some of the clearest evidence yet that many of these innovations emerged well before the rise of modern mammals." The research also has important implications for understanding living mammals. While therian mammals use a sophisticated suckling mechanism supported by the soft palate and constrictor muscles, monotremes such as platypuses and echidnas use a different method for obtaining milk and lack some of these anatomical features. The new evidence suggests that monotremes likely lost elements of the ancestral suckling apparatus during their evolutionary history and developed an alternative method of milk intake. Beyond feeding biology, Megacauda highlights the remarkable ecological diversity of mammaliaforms living alongside dinosaurs. At approximately the size of a modern otter, it is among the largest known Jurassic mammaliaforms and represents one of the earliest examples of adaptation to a semiaquatic lifestyle. "These discoveries continue to reveal that the age of dinosaurs was also a time of extraordinary evolutionary innovation among early mammals," said Peishu Li, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine and a co-author of the study. cards.headline: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus

image.alt: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus

pages.text:
Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. cards.headline: Newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, Wales, may validate medieval folklore

image.alt: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

pages.text: Archaeologists have discovered a Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, Wales, that may provide physical evidence for a medieval legend regarding the fourth-century Roman emperor Magnus Maximus. The site, located approximately 2 miles (3.5km) southwest of the Frenni Fawr summit, contains fourth-century coins and other artifacts that suggest the medieval tales of the emperor's military camp were rooted in reality. Previously, there had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on or below the summit of Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills. The discovery was made in 2024 by Dr. Mark Merrony, a Roman specialist at the University of Oxford, who identified a potential outline via satellite imagery in an overgrown field before finding Roman tiles on the ground.

The find relates to the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales involving myth, magic, and miracles. Specifically, the story *The Dream of Macsen Wledig* describes the emperor—referred to by his Welsh name—pitching a military camp at Frenni Fawr during his maneuvers. While Magnus Maximus is known to have led troops against the Picts and Scots in the fourth century, the theory that he established a camp near this specific hill had been based solely on this folklore. Dr. Merrony, who heads the excavation, noted that this landscape contains the only Roman military site close to the location described in the Mabinogion, suggesting the presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help resolve the mystery of the nearly 1,700-year-old legend.

cards.headline: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow by up to 45% and alters neural communication

image.alt: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication

pages.text: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a brain-imaging study presented at the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology (ECNP) Congress in Munich. Researchers suggest that the intensity of the resulting altered states of consciousness may be linked more closely to changes in how brain networks communicate than to the reduction in blood flow alone. This finding challenges the common explanation that breathwork experiences are caused simply by the brain receiving less blood. During the study, 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners performed high-ventilation breathing while undergoing MRI scanning. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by approximately 45% on average, dropping from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min during the session. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly 'oceanic state'—a deep feeling of connection to the universe—that resembled the effects of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, though with less pronounced visual effects. They also reported altered perception, vivid mental imagery, and changes in self-experience.

The study found that individuals who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, a system of brain regions involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. Dr. Christian Schmitz, lead researcher from the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim, Germany, stated that while many practitioners report profound changes in perception, the underlying mechanisms have been poorly understood. He noted that these experiences appear linked to both marked changes in cerebral blood flow and alterations in how key brain networks communicate. Co-coordinator Hana Adolphi described breathwork as a legal, inexpensive, and non-pharmacological intervention that could serve as a tool for studying altered states of consciousness and informing future mental health treatments. However, she noted the study was relatively small and the findings are preliminary, requiring larger studies to determine clinical relevance. Dr. Guy Fincham of Brighton and Sussex Medical School, who was not involved in the study, noted the research was uncontrolled and used experienced practitioners. He suggested that replication in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomized-controlled design is necessary to determine if these findings translate more widely for therapeutic benefit. David Nutt, a professor at Imperial College London who was also not involved, described breathwork as a non-pharmacological bridge to research into psychedelics.
